card.hook: Picture a weekend cabin that grabs a waterfall and just sits on it. Long concrete terraces stretch out into the trees with nothing holding up the far end, and your phone is going to love those lines.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 40 m north-west of the subject, and face south-east towards Fallingwater. If trees block part of the view, take a few steps to either side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole house and its terraces in one go, since you're fairly close. Then try 1x for a natural look, and zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the stonework, the glass and the terrace edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the long terrace edges with them, so those horizontal lines stay nice and level.
card.best_time: The house sits under a forest canopy, so expect dappled light and lots of green whenever you go. The stream can freeze in winter and dry up in summer, so the waterfall won't always look the same. Check the official site for visiting times before you set out.
card.selfie_here: Head for the 'Overlook' after your tour by following the 'View' arrows along the trail through the woods. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and turn so the house and Bear Run's waterfall sit behind your shoulder in that classic postcard angle.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the driveway approach at the bridge leading to the entrance and look back, so you're in front of the house, seen from the southeast side.
card.rules_and_safety: No drones on the grounds. Inside the house, photos are flash-free and only when your tour guide says so, and please don't block walkways. Bring a light jacket and comfy shoes, because the weather can change in minutes.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole house, then find three different textures up close: stone, glass and concrete. Bonus points if one has a leaf in it.
card.good_to_know: Frank Lloyd Wright designed Fallingwater as a weekend retreat for Edgar J. Kaufmann Sr. and his wife Liliane, and the Kaufmanns began using it in 1937. It's built partly over a waterfall on Bear Run, from local stone, reinforced concrete, steel and plate glass. The Western Pennsylvania Conservancy has run it as a visitor attraction since 1963, and it's a National Historic Landmark and part of a World Heritage Site.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 40 m north-west of the subject, and face south-east towards Fallingwater. If trees block part of the view, take a few steps to either side.

selfie_research.notes: Coordinates were not confirmed by any page; the site is at 1491 Mill Run Road, Mill Run, PA, so check the position against that address. Sources conflict on tripods: the official policy allows them outside, while the visitor information and tours pages ban them inside. One blog (2018) says the most iconic photo spot is not open to the public and visitors must shoot from a viewpoint a couple hundred yards away, so the Overlook may be the closest public option. Interior photo rules differ by tour type, and older sources say photos are allowed only on the first floor or on premium tours; check the current policy before going.

card.hook: Here's a surprise: the best view of this Frank Lloyd Wright house is from the back, where the low stone walls and the broad copper roof look like they grew out of the hillside.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kentuck Knob Overlook, about 100 m south-east of the house, and face north-west. You'll see the rear of the house with its sandstone walls and cantilevered roof, and the Youghiogheny River gorge and Laurel Highlands ridges behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the house and ridges together. If you're close and the roof gets chopped off, drop to 0.5x. Try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the stone and the copper roof edge.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the roofline along the upper third with the ridges above it, and keep the horizon level, because that long roof shows every tilt.
card.best_time: A bright overcast day is ideal. The soft light keeps hard shadows from pooling under the roof overhang. In autumn, the leaf colour could add some warmth to the trees around the house.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x on Kentuck Knob Overlook, or on the flagstone back patio by the triangular pond where the tour lets out. Tilt the phone so the house sits over your shoulder. Trees can screen the gorge, so expect ridges and treetops behind you rather than a big river view.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand in the courtyard facing the carport and main entrance, with the stone fences at either side of the frame, while you pose near the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: No photography is allowed inside the house, but outdoor photos are fine. Some steps at the start of the sculpture-garden walk could be tricky for visitors with mobility issues. The house is open for tours, and it's not clear whether the overlook or hillside can be used without a tour ticket, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the long roofline sitting perfectly level on a gridline, then take a second shot with the roof tucked in behind your head.
card.good_to_know: Frank Lloyd Wright designed this small house for I. N. Hagan, an ice-cream company owner, and his wife Bernardine. It was finished in 1956, built of local stone and redwood with a copper roof, and its plan is built around a hexagon. The Hagans first heard of Wright through the family who built Fallingwater, and the house is now a National Historic Landmark.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Kentuck Knob Overlook, about 100 m south-east of the house, and face north-west. You'll see the rear of the house with its sandstone walls and cantilevered roof, and the Youghiogheny River gorge and Laurel Highlands ridges behind it.

card.hook: These falls are only about 20 feet (6 m) high, yet they're the most photographed spot in the whole park. The trick is that they stretch right across the river, so your picture is all about width and rushing white water.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Ohiopyle Falls Observation Deck, right beside the parking lot on Main Street (Route 381). Face the river and you'll see the full width of the falls, with the tree-covered Ferncliff Peninsula behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the whole sweep of the falls and the forest. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look, and zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the white water or the Ferncliff trees.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the lip of the falls along a lower line, so the water fills the frame and the trees sit above it.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon. The light is softer and there's less glare bouncing off the water.
card.selfie_here: Try Ferncliff Overlook, on the Ferncliff Trail side of the river. Walk down from the Ferncliff Trail lot, about a tenth of a mile past the side view of the falls. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the falls behind you; one blogger calls it one of the best selfie spots in the park.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in front of the Laurel Highlands Visitors Center, which shares the deck's parking lot, for a shot that shows how big the falls look behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The rock ledge on the Ferncliff Trail is described as a precarious viewpoint, so keep back from the edge when posing. The falls area was reported as being rebuilt, so check current construction and parking before you go.
card.challenge: Take one super-wide shot of the whole falls, then walk closer and see if you can catch just the froth. Which one looks more like 'it turns very white'?
card.good_to_know: Ohiopyle comes from a Lenape phrase meaning 'it turns very white', which suits the frothy water. The park opened to the public in 1965 and was formally dedicated in 1971. The Fallingwater house is several miles away, so this card is all about the falls.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Ohiopyle Falls Observation Deck, right beside the parking lot on Main Street (Route 381). Face the river and you'll see the full width of the falls, with the tree-covered Ferncliff Peninsula behind.

The sources do not say where the visitor should stand in the passer-by shot, only that the visitor center view gives a better sense of scale. I found no page stating selfie-stick or tripod rules for Ohiopyle State Park; the Disney rules I found apply to theme parks, not this park, so I left the rules list empty. The sources are blogs and a tour company, and one of the Ferncliff spots is a steep, rocky hike.

card.hook: Most people see this bridge from the top, walking across it. Down on the Ferncliff Trail you get to crane your neck instead, and the long steel deck floats high above the river like it's showing off.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Ferncliff Trail, on the Ferncliff Peninsula by the riverbank, and face up at the bridge from below. Keep the high steel deck in the upper part of your frame, with the gorge, river and trees underneath.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole deck, gorge and trees into one shot. Then try 1x for a calmer look at the span. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the steel high above.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the deck along the upper third line, and keep your phone level so the bridge doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Autumn is the star here, because the trees add colour to the view from the trail. Earlier or later in the day, the softer light usually suits a bridge against the sky better than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, go to the High Ohiopyle Bridge Scenic View Area, the overlook on the Great Allegheny Passage trail just before the bridge's open end. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if your phone offers it) and frame yourself in the bridge's opening with the river gorge behind you.
card.ask_someone: Want a photo of you with the bridge? Ask a passer-by on the Ferncliff riverbank trail to shoot upward while you stand below the bridge.
card.rules_and_safety: The Ferncliff Trail can flood in high water, so check the official site before you go. Keep your phone strapped or held firmly when you're near the edge of the water.
card.challenge: Find the gap in the trees that frames the deck like a picture frame, then take the shot with the bridge dead level.
card.good_to_know: The bridge opened in 1912 as part of the Western Maryland Railway, the last major railroad built in Pennsylvania. It stands more than 100 feet higher than the nearby Ohiopyle Low Bridge. It was rehabilitated and reopened for public use in 1989, and now carries the Great Allegheny Passage trail.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Ferncliff Trail, on the Ferncliff Peninsula by the riverbank, and face up at the bridge from below. Keep the high steel deck in the upper part of your frame, with the gorge, river and trees underneath.

selfie_research.notes: Only the first selfie spot is clearly tied to the bridge in frame; the second is a mural photo, and the ask-someone spot is a photographer's vantage from below that a page shows, not a page-stated posing spot for a visitor. The GPS coordinates on the 5 Instagram page (39.85707, -70.46388) look mistyped and do not match the given position, so I did not use them. The 'City' given as Fallingwater is a house near Mill Run, not Ohiopyle; the given coordinates fit Ohiopyle, where the bridge sits. The drone rules I found (Ohio Administrative Code 1501:46-13-11 and related Ohio pages) apply to Ohio state parks, and Ohiopyle is in Pennsylvania, so I have not reported them as rules here. No page I found mentions selfie sticks or tripods. Several pages are several years old, so check current conditions with Ohiopyle State Park.
